# Weekly Market Performance — November 20, 2026


[LPL Research](https://www.lpl.com/research/research-team/lpl-research.html)


Last Updated: November 20, 2026


**LPL Research provides its Weekly Market Performance for the week of November 16, 2026.** Artificial intelligence (AI) uncertainty remained the dominant market theme as ongoing AI buildout and financing concerns outweighed reassurance from NVIDIA’s (NVDA) earnings and Anthropic’s (ANT) successful debut. Simultaneously, selling broadened beyond technology shares, providing less padding for losses. European and Asian equities also dropped, while Treasuries advanced on a fresh haven bid despite hawkish-tilted Federal Reserve (Fed) takeaways. Dollar strength provided another headwind across assets, while losses in metals and crude oil weighed on the commodity complex.

## U.S. and International Equities


**U.S. Equities:** Stocks remained under pressure for another week as markets continued to work through a dizzying month of post-midterm uncertainty, high-profile tech earnings, an AI leadership vacuum, worries about peaking capital expenditures (capex), and liquidity challenges following the largest initial public offering (IPO) in history. Sentiment was cautious entering the week ahead of NVDA’s quarterly report and the much-anticipated ANT IPO. NVDA's beat and raise Tuesday evening provided some reassurance on AI demand, however, questions around the chipmaking giant's longer-term growth and export controls erased a brief bounce attempt across AI names.


Selling pressure lingered and the S&P 500 extended its losing streak to seven straight sessions through week's end after ANT's successful listing, widely expected to be a clearing event, instead seemed to kindle some worries of competitive positioning and pricing power across the AI ecosystem. While global investors unwound AI exposure, major U.S. averages were also dented as the strong breadth that has cushioned losses recently faded, giving way to wider selling which left over 70% of S&P 500 shares lower three out of five days this week. Prospects of tightening global monetary policy and a stronger dollar added to broader pressure.


**International Equities:** European equities fared better than their counterparts across the pond, but the STOXX 600 still ended the week sharply lower. Resilience as an AI rotation beneficiary limited Monday's drop, however, defensive sectors that helped prop up the regional benchmark fell as global markets' tone turned risk-off. Weakness in mining shares amid a drop in metals prices was also a headwind, while an upward revision to October core consumer inflation and fresh threats from Russia toward Ukraine tamped down broader sentiment across the Eurozone. The U.K. was a relative bright spot, outperforming on limited tech exposure and a retail sales beat.


Meanwhile, Asia-Pacific equities led losses for global regions as regional benchmarks dropped the most since March 2020. Tech-heavy exchanges felt the most pressure amid the global unwind of AI trades, while concerns of more stringent U.S. export controls added to anxious sentiment around tech sector revenue and computing capacity. Taiwan led losses with a 17.5% rout amid headlines of foreign investor selling, while South Korea followed with an 8% retreat. Greater China outperformed as U.S. chip restriction jitters was partially countered by expectations for an acceleration in domestic chip development. Japanese benchmarks stumbled, with additional pressure from competition concerns after SK Hynix announced plans to open a new testing facility, and weakness in banking names. India bucked the trend with a fourth straight weekly gain.


## Fixed Income, Currency, and Commodity Markets


**Fixed Income:** Core bonds, measured by the Bloomberg U.S. Aggregate Index traded higher this week, buoyed by a late-week flight to safety in Treasuries. This week's advance marks six in the last seven, with last week the exception. The return of haven demand for Treasuries came despite hawkish-tilted meeting minutes and another wave of hawkish Fed-speak over the last five days in which Fed officials increasingly signaled they are debating how much to raise rates, not whether. This Treasury market resilience partly reflects expectations for further tightening already priced into yields, but a larger-than-expected hike remains a risk, leaving the front end sensitive to incoming data.


At the same time, AI is now part of the Fed’s inflation and financial-stability discussion. Officials identified AI-related demand as a potential source of inflation pressure, while Fed staff highlighted the rapid growth of debt tied to the AI buildout. And on the corporate side, NVDA's earnings confirmed strong AI demand, but strong technology demand does not remove credit risk or automatically make every company financing that demand a strong credit. Bottom line, a Fed leaning toward tighter policy and a credit market becoming more discriminating about AI financing argue for selectivity for investors.


**Commodities and Currencies:** The broader commodities complex traded lower for a fifth consecutive week. Selling spread across the complex over the last five days with precious metals facing the largest downside. Gold prices tumbled near $3,500/ounce, its lowest level in over a year, marking a decisive break below the $4,000/ounce level which was expected to act as a floor supported by central bank buying and dip buying. The yellow metal was also caught up in the global equity market sell-off as investors covered losses with bullion, while hawkish Fed takeaways added to headwinds alongside continued strength in the U.S. dollar, which makes gold more expensive for most buyers. Silver also tumbled as froth continued to be removed from prices, while copper sank as AI worries spurred speculation around the red metal's data center-backed demand story. Elsewhere, crude fell for a third week as U.S.-Iran headlines fell quiet outside of the White House stating there is no rush on a decision. Russia-Ukraine tensions capped losses, but the U.S. Energy Secretary downplaying supply and shipment concerns and an agreement between the U.S., Russia, and China to increase production provided an offset.


## Economic Weekly Roundup


The release of the October Fed meeting minutes offered no surprises as policymakers appear firmly committed to additional tightening, with the debate shifting from whether to raise rates to how dramatically. Since the inflation data will likely improve in November and December, the FOMC will hike by 25 basis points (0.25%) and will not likely feel the need to hike by a larger magnitude.


This week's economic calendar was also highlighted by October retail sales numbers suggesting American consumers remain willing to spend, even as higher prices continue to squeeze purchasing power. Based on the data from the U.S. Census Bureau, dining out remains a priority as restaurant spending rose more than 7% annually, its strongest pace in over three years. Online spending continues to surge as non-store retail sales climbed 11.8% from a year ago, the second consecutive double-digit increase. Bottom line, consumer demand remains remarkably resilient, with discretionary spending holding up despite higher prices and persistent inflation. Given the stability of the broader consumer, the Fed will likely focus on its inflation mandate. If this trend in retail sales continues and the labor market holds, expect another hike in Q1 next year.
